paragraphs: I argued in an earlier chapter that people cannot do without firm beliefs, and that it is very much to be desired that they hold them. I now add that, of all the kinds of firm belief, the one that seems to me most desirable is firm belief in matters of religion. This follows clearly even if we consider nothing higher than the interests of this world. Hardly any human action, however particular its character, fails to originate in some very general idea that people have formed of God, of his relation to humanity, of the nature of their own souls, and of their duties to their fellow human beings. Nothing can prevent these ideas from being the common source from which everything else flows. People therefore have an immense stake in acquiring fixed ideas of God, of the soul, and of their common duties to their Creator and to one another. For doubt about these first principles would leave all their actions to the impulse of chance, and would condemn them to live, to a certain extent, powerless and undisciplined.

This, then, is the subject on which it is most important for each of us to hold fixed ideas. Unhappily, it is also the subject on which it is hardest for each of us, left alone, to settle our opinions by the force of reason alone. Only minds unusually free from the ordinary anxieties of life, minds that are at once penetrating, subtle, and trained in thinking, can sound the depths of these most necessary truths, and even they need much time and care to do it. Indeed, we see that these philosophers are themselves almost always wrapped in uncertainties. At every step the natural light that illuminates their path grows dimmer and less secure. In spite of all their efforts, they have so far discovered only a small number of conflicting ideas, on which the human mind has been tossed about for thousands of years without getting a firmer grip on the truth or even finding anything new in its errors. Studies of this kind are far above the average capacity of people. And even if most of mankind were capable of such pursuits, it is clear that they would still lack the leisure to pursue them. Fixed ideas of God and of human nature are indispensable to the daily conduct of people’s lives, but the conduct of their lives prevents them from acquiring such ideas.

I think the difficulty has no parallel. Among the sciences, some are useful to the mass of mankind and within its reach. Others can be approached only by a few, and the many do not study them, since they need nothing beyond their more remote applications. But the daily practice of the science I am speaking of is indispensable to everyone, even though the study of it is out of reach for the great majority.

General ideas about God and human nature are therefore, above all others, the ideas that it is most fitting to withdraw from the habitual action of private judgment, and the ones in which there is most to gain and least to lose by recognizing a principle of authority. The first object of religions, and one of their principal advantages, is to give each of these fundamental questions an answer that is clear, precise, intelligible to the mass of mankind, and lasting. Some religions are very false and very absurd. Yet it may be affirmed that any religion that stays within the circle I have just traced, without aspiring to go beyond it (as many religions have tried to do, in order to fence in the free progress of the human mind on every side), imposes a salutary restraint on the intellect. And it must be admitted that, even if such a religion does not save people in another world, it is at least very conducive to their happiness and greatness in this one. This is especially true of people living in free countries. When a people’s religion is destroyed, doubt takes hold of the highest part of the intellect and half paralyzes all the rest of its powers. Everyone grows used to holding only confused and shifting ideas on the subjects that matter most to himself and his fellow human beings. His opinions are poorly defended and easily abandoned. Despairing of ever solving by himself the hardest problems of human destiny, he ignobly resigns himself to thinking no more about them. Such a condition cannot fail to weaken the soul, loosen the springs of the will, and prepare a people for servitude. In such a case people do not merely allow their freedom to be wrested from them; they often give it up themselves. When there is no longer any principle of authority in religion, any more than in politics, people are soon frightened by the sight of this unbounded independence. The constant agitation of everything around them alarms and exhausts them. Since everything in the realm of the intellect is adrift, they decide at least that the machinery of society should be firm and fixed. And since they cannot return to their old belief, they take a master.

For my own part, I doubt that a person can ever bear complete religious independence and entire public freedom at the same time. And I am inclined to think that if he lacks faith, he must serve, and if he is free, he must believe.

Perhaps, however, this great usefulness of religions is even more obvious among nations where equality of conditions prevails than among others. It must be acknowledged that equality, though it brings great benefits into the world, also suggests to people (as will be shown later) some very dangerous tendencies. It tends to isolate them from one another and to fix each person’s attention on himself, and it opens the soul to an immoderate love of material gratification. The greatest advantage of religion is that it inspires exactly the opposite principles. There is no religion that does not place the object of human desire above and beyond the treasures of the earth, and that does not naturally lift the soul to regions far above those of the senses. Nor is there any that does not impose on a person some duties toward his fellow human beings, and so draw him at times out of the contemplation of himself. This is true even of the most false and dangerous religions. Religious nations are therefore naturally strong at the very point where democratic nations are weak. This shows how important it is for people to keep their religion as their conditions become more equal.

I have neither the right nor the intention to examine the supernatural means by which God instills religious belief in the human heart. At this moment I am considering religions from a purely human point of view. My aim is to ask by what means they can most easily keep their hold in the democratic ages we are entering. It has been shown that in times of general education and equality, the human mind accepts firm opinions only with reluctance, and feels the need of them keenly only in spiritual matters. This proves, first, that in such times religions ought to confine themselves within their own bounds more carefully than at any other time. For in seeking to extend their power beyond religious matters, they risk not being believed at all. The circle within which they try to confine the human intellect should therefore be drawn carefully, and beyond its edge the mind should be left entirely free to follow its own guidance. Muhammad claimed to receive from Heaven, and put into the Koran, not only a body of religious doctrines but also political maxims, civil and criminal laws, and theories of science. The Gospel, by contrast, speaks only of the general relations of people to God and to one another, and beyond that it teaches and imposes no article of faith. This alone, besides a thousand other reasons, would be enough to prove that the first of these religions will never long dominate an educated and democratic age, while the second is destined to keep its hold in such an age as in all others.

But to pursue this part of the subject, I find that for religions to keep their authority, humanly speaking, in democratic ages, they must do more than confine themselves strictly to the circle of spiritual matters. Their power also depends very much on the nature of the belief they teach, on the external forms they take, and on the obligations they impose. My earlier observation that equality leads people to very general and very broad ideas applies principally to the question of religion. People who live in a similar and equal condition in the world easily conceive the idea of one God, who governs every person by the same laws and grants every person future happiness on the same terms. The idea of the unity of mankind constantly leads them back to the idea of the unity of the Creator. In a state of society where people are broken up into very unequal ranks, by contrast, they tend to invent as many deities as there are nations, castes, classes, or families, and to trace out a thousand private roads to heaven.

It cannot be denied that Christianity itself has felt, to a certain extent, the influence that social and political conditions have on religious opinions. When the Christian religion appeared on earth, Providence, which had doubtless prepared the world for its coming, had gathered a large part of the human race, like an immense flock, under the scepter of the Caesars. The people who made up this multitude differed in many ways, but they had this much in common: they all obeyed the same laws, and every subject was so weak and insignificant beside the imperial ruler that all appeared equal when their condition was compared with his. This new and peculiar state of mankind necessarily predisposed people to listen to the general truths that Christianity teaches, and it may help explain the ease and speed with which those truths then penetrated the human mind. The opposite state of things appeared after the destruction of the empire. The Roman world was then, as it were, shattered into a thousand fragments, and each nation went back to its original individuality. An endless scale of ranks soon grew up within these nations. The different races were more sharply defined, and castes divided each nation into several peoples. In the midst of this common effort, which seemed to drive human society toward the greatest imaginable degree of voluntary subdivision, Christianity did not lose sight of the leading general ideas it had brought into the world. But it seemed nonetheless to adapt itself, as far as it could, to the new tendencies that the fragmentation of mankind had produced. People continued to worship one God, the Creator and Preserver of all things. But every people, every city, and, so to speak, every individual thought of obtaining some distinct privilege and winning the favor of a special patron at the foot of the Throne of Grace. Unable to divide the Deity, they multiplied the divine agents and wrongly inflated their importance. The homage due to saints and angels became an almost idolatrous worship for most of the Christian world, and for a moment there was reason to fear that the religion of Christ would slide back toward the superstitions it had conquered. It seems clear that the more the barriers are removed that separate nation from nation among mankind, and citizen from citizen within a people, the stronger the human mind’s bent becomes, as if by its own impulse, toward the idea of a single, all-powerful Being who dispenses equal laws in the same way to every person. In democratic ages, then, it is especially important not to let the homage paid to secondary agents be confused with the worship due to the Creator alone.

Another truth is no less clear: religions ought to take on fewer external observances in democratic periods than in any others. In speaking of philosophical method among the Americans, I showed that in an age of equality nothing is more repugnant to the human mind than the idea of submitting to forms. People living in such times are impatient with figures of speech. To them, symbols seem a childish device for hiding or dressing up truths that would more naturally be laid bare in the light of day. They are unmoved by ceremonial observances, and they are inclined to give only secondary importance to the details of public worship. Those who have the task of regulating the external forms of religion in a democratic age should pay close attention to these natural tendencies of the human mind, so as not to run against them needlessly. I firmly believe in the necessity of forms, which hold the human mind fixed on the contemplation of abstract truths, spur its ardor in pursuing them, and strengthen its power to hold them steadily. Nor do I suppose that it is possible to maintain a religion without external observances. But on the other hand, I am convinced that in the ages we are entering it would be especially dangerous to multiply them beyond measure, and that they should rather be limited to what is absolutely necessary to perpetuate the doctrine itself, which is the substance of religions, of which the ritual is only the form. *a A religion that became more minute, more rigid, and more loaded with petty observances at a time when people are becoming more equal would soon find itself reduced to a band of fanatical zealots in the midst of an unbelieving people.

[Footnote a: In all religions there are some ceremonies which are inherent in the substance of the faith itself, and in these nothing should, on any account, be changed. This is especially the case with Roman Catholicism, in which the doctrine and the form are frequently so closely united as to form one point of belief.]

I anticipate the objection that, since all religions have general and eternal truths as their object, they cannot adapt themselves to the shifting spirit of every age without giving up their claim to certainty in the eyes of mankind. To this I reply again that the principal opinions that make up belief, which theologians call articles of faith, must be carefully distinguished from the accessories attached to them. Religions are obliged to hold fast to the former, whatever the particular spirit of the age. But they should take good care not to bind themselves in the same way to the latter, at a time when everything is in transition, and when the mind, accustomed to the moving pageant of human affairs, reluctantly puts up with any attempt to fix it to a given point. The fixity of external and secondary things can offer a chance of lasting only when civil society is itself fixed. Under any other circumstances I consider it perilous.

We shall have occasion to see that, of all the passions that originate in equality or are fostered by it, there is one that it makes especially intense, and that it instills at the same time in the heart of every person. I mean the love of well-being. The taste for well-being is the prominent and indelible feature of democratic ages. It may be believed that a religion that undertook to destroy so deep-seated a passion would in the end be destroyed by it. And if such a religion tried to wean people entirely from thinking about the good things of this world, in order to devote their faculties exclusively to thinking about another, it can be foreseen that the soul would eventually escape its grasp and plunge into the exclusive enjoyment of present, material pleasures. The chief concern of religions is to purify, regulate, and restrain the excessive and exclusive taste for well-being that people feel in periods of equality. But they would be mistaken to try to control it completely or to root it out. They will not succeed in curing people of the love of riches, but they can still persuade them to enrich themselves only by honest means.

This brings me to a final consideration, which includes, as it were, all the others. The more the conditions of people are equalized and made alike, the more important it is for religions, while they carefully keep out of the daily turmoil of secular affairs, not to run needlessly against the ideas that generally prevail or the permanent interests that exist among the mass of the people. For as public opinion grows more and more clearly the first and most irresistible of existing powers, the religious principle has no outside support strong enough to let it resist public opinion’s attacks for long. This is just as true of a democratic people ruled by a despot as of a republic. In ages of equality, kings may often command obedience, but the majority always commands belief. Deference is therefore to be paid to the majority in everything that is not contrary to the faith.

I showed in my earlier volumes how the American clergy keep aloof from secular affairs. This is the most obvious example of their self-restraint, but it is not the only one. In America, religion is a separate sphere, in which the priest is sovereign but which he takes care never to leave. Within its limits he is master of the mind. Beyond them he leaves people to themselves and surrenders them to the independence and instability that belong to their nature and their age. I have seen no country in which Christianity is clothed with fewer forms, figures, and observances than in the United States, or where it presents the mind with ideas that are more distinct, more simple, or more general. Although the Christians of America are divided into a multitude of sects, they all look at their religion in the same light. This applies to Roman Catholicism as well as to the other forms of belief. There are no Roman priests who show less taste for minute individual observances, for extraordinary or peculiar means of salvation, or who cling more to the spirit and less to the letter of the law, than the Roman Catholic priests of the United States. Nowhere is the Church’s doctrine that forbids offering to the saints the worship reserved for God alone more clearly taught or more generally followed. Yet the Roman Catholics of America are very submissive and very sincere.

Another remark applies to the clergy of every denomination. The American ministers of the gospel do not try to draw all of a person’s thoughts toward the life to come or to fix them there. They are willing to leave a portion of his heart to the cares of the present, and they seem to regard the goods of this world as important, though secondary, objects. If they take no part themselves in productive labor, they are at least interested in its progress and ready to applaud its results. And while they never cease to point to the other world as the great object of the believer’s hopes and fears, they do not forbid him to seek prosperity honestly in this one. Far from trying to show that these things are separate and opposed to each other, they rather study to find the point at which they are most closely connected.

All the American clergy know and respect the intellectual supremacy exercised by the majority, and they engage in only those conflicts with it that are necessary. They take no part in the quarrels of parties, but they readily adopt the general opinions of their country and their age. They let themselves be carried along, without resistance, in the current of feeling and opinion that sweeps along everything around them. They try to improve their contemporaries, but they do not break off fellowship with them. Public opinion is therefore never hostile to them; it rather supports and protects them. Their belief owes its authority both to the strength that is its own and to the strength that it borrows from the opinions of the majority. Thus, by respecting all democratic tendencies that are not absolutely contrary to herself, and by making use of several of them for her own purposes, religion carries on an advantageous struggle against that spirit of individual independence which is her most dangerous opponent.
